steps/chain: In the chain rule, x fed one simple function, and its output, u, fed the next. Each link was simple, with a slope you knew.
steps/more: Most formulas are not one straight chain. This one takes three inputs, x, z and c, and their paths join.
steps/wengert: In 1964, R. E. Wengert, at General Electric, showed how a computer can take any formula apart: into a series of elementary steps, each a single simple operation.
steps/list: Here, the steps are: multiply x by z, and call it q. Add c to q, and call that r. Square r, and that is f.
steps/why: Then nothing is handled all at once: each step is simple enough to compute, and to find the slope of, on its own.
graph/mul: Now draw the steps. The multiply becomes a circle, called a node, with x and z coming in along wires, and q going out.
graph/add: q travels along a wire into an add node, which also takes c, and sends out r.
graph/sq: And a square node turns r into f, the output.
graph/name: Nodes joined by wires make a graph: not a plotted curve, but dots joined by lines. This one computes, so it is called a computational graph.
graph/count: One node per operation: three operations, three nodes. A formula that added twice would get two add nodes.
graph/ends: The inputs are not nodes: they are where values come in. And f is just what the last node sends out.
forward/inputs: To evaluate the graph, give the inputs values: x is two, z is three, and c is minus four.
forward/mul: Values flow forward, from the inputs toward the output. The multiply gives two times three: six.
forward/add: The add gives six plus minus four: two. It never sees x or z, only q, the one value the multiply sent.
forward/sq: And the square gives two squared: four. So f is four.
forward/ready: The order is forced. A node can run only once every value it needs has arrived, so the add waits for the multiply, and the square waits for the add.
forward/pass: One trip through the nodes in that order, inputs to output, is called the forward pass.
forward/again: Change x to three, and run the forward pass again. Every value that depends on x changes, and f becomes twenty five.
more/max: Two more kinds of node. A max node passes on the larger of its inputs, written max of x and z: the max of one and minus two is one.
more/exp: An exponential node raises e to its input: e to the one is about two point seven two.
more/share: And one input can feed two nodes: z goes into the max, and also into the multiply at the end. Two wires, but still no node of its own.
more/mul: The multiply gives two point seven two times minus two: about minus five point four four.
more/pieces: Add, multiply, max, exp and square: from a handful of pieces like these, every formula here is built.
